tip: wrth eu bodd means delighted, literally at their pleasure. The possessive tracks the subject, so the children take eu, their.
Fronting the pronoun adds emphasis: Nhw oedd means it was them who did it, stronger than a plain they had.
Welsh has no verb for prefer. It uses gwell gan, better with someone: well ganddi de means she prefers tea.
ymweld, to visit, takes â (with) before its object: ymweld â'i rhieni, visit her parents, never a direct object.
To say bring, Welsh uses dod â, literally come with: dod â'r pwdin means bring the dessert.
erbyn means by, as in by a deadline something must be done: erbyn dydd Gwener, by Friday.
After os (if), Welsh uses a short verb for the future: cloi di means if you lock, no separate word for will.
For a duration still going on, use ers with a perfect: wedi bod yn sâl ers deuddydd, have been ill for two days.
Oni bai am means but for, or if it weren't for: Oni bai am y glaw sets up an unreal cause, the rain that did happen.
In reported speech, that is fod, from bod: Dywedodd... fod yr ysgol, said that the school, links the two clauses.
Pe baen ni means if we, marking an unreal or hypothetical if rather than a likely one: Pe baen ni'n byw, if we lived.
Cod dy galon literally means lift your heart, the everyday Welsh for chin up or take heart.
Carwn i is a polite I would like, the conditional of caru: Carwn i eich gwahodd, I would like to invite you.
The position word i (to) softens the next consonant, so Caerfyrddin becomes i Gaerfyrddin, c turning to g.
ca i is the short future of the irregular cael, to get: os ca i'r swydd means if I get the job.
Welsh forms the passive with cael plus a possessive: cael ei gwblhau, literally get its completing, means be completed.
hynaf means oldest, the superlative of hen, old. Welsh superlatives usually end in -af.
For an indirect yes-or-no question, whether is a: a fydd y diwygiadau, whether the reforms will.
